Q011870:
## Why the data size decides
Single-node libraries such as scikit-learn load the whole training matrix into the memory of one machine (on Databricks, the driver). Databricks recommends keeping training on one machine when possible, because distributed code is more complex and slower from communication overhead, but says to consider distributed training when the data or model is too large to fit in memory on a single machine.
## What Spark ML adds
Spark ML (`pyspark.ml`, the DataFrame-based MLlib API) runs each algorithm as Spark jobs: rows stay in partitions on the workers, and each iteration aggregates partial results (for example gradients) instead of collecting the data. Adding workers adds memory and compute. The same `Pipeline` also runs where the data already lives, so there is no copy to the driver.
- Choose Spark ML when the training data cannot fit on one node, when the features are produced by Spark transformations on a big table, or when scoring happens inside Spark jobs.
- Choose a single node (scikit-learn, XGBoost, PyTorch) when the data fits comfortably and you need an algorithm or accuracy that Spark ML does not offer.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Swap space:** paging a training matrix from disk makes each pass over the data orders of magnitude slower and is not a supported way to extend memory; it does not give a usable nightly job.
- ✗ **B. 0.1% sample:** a sample can be a valid choice when a learning curve is flat, but here the requirement explicitly needs the full history and rare segments, and a 0.1% sample would drop them.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** A Spark ML pipeline is the design that scales with the data. The 1.2 billion rows never leave the workers, the logistic regression is trained by the distributed solver, and the fitted `PipelineModel` can score on the same cluster.
- ✗ **D. toPandas on the driver:** `toPandas()` collects every row to the driver process, so it fails with out-of-memory exactly because the data is larger than the largest node.

## Key idea
When the training data does not fit on one node, use a distributed library such as Spark ML; otherwise stay on a single node.
Q011871:
## Fit the tool to the data and the algorithm
The 3 GB table fits easily in memory on one node. Distributed training pays communication and scheduling costs in every iteration, so for data this small a single node is usually faster and simpler. A model that already beats the Spark ML alternatives is a second reason to keep it.
## A common split of work
- Use Spark for what it is good at: reading, joining and aggregating the large source tables into a feature table.
- Convert the finished feature table to pandas (`toPandas()` or the Spark-to-pandas Arrow path) and train on a single node with the library the team trusts.
- Revisit Spark ML or another distributed option (Ray, TorchDistributor for neural networks) only when the data or model no longer fits on one machine.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Linear regression only:** Spark ML has many families (trees, ensembles, GBT, ALS, KMeans); the claim is false, and switching to a linear model would likely lose accuracy.
- ✗ **B. Rewrite as GBTRegressor:** distributed training is not always faster. On 3 GB the per-iteration communication outweighs the gain, and the team has measured that Spark ML does not reach the same error.
- ✗ **C. Training inside mapInPandas:** `mapInPandas` runs a function on each partition independently, so each worker would train its own separate model on a slice; it does not combine them into one model.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Preparing features in Spark and training scikit-learn on a single node keeps the better algorithm, avoids distribution overhead on 3 GB, and leaves a clear trigger (data outgrowing memory) for moving to Spark ML.

## Key idea
When the data fits on one node and the single-node algorithm is better, use Spark for data preparation and train on a single node.
Q011872:
## Spark ML parallelism follows partitions
Spark ML algorithms run as ordinary Spark jobs: one task processes one partition of the training DataFrame, and the iterative or per-level aggregation happens across those tasks. If the DataFrame has 8 partitions, at most 8 cores work on each pass, however large the cluster is.
## What to check
- Compare the number of tasks in the Spark UI stage with the total executor cores.
- Repartition to a small multiple of the core count (`df.repartition(320)`) so all cores get work and one slow partition does not dominate.
- Cache the repartitioned DataFrame when the algorithm makes many passes (random forest levels, logistic regression iterations), so the shuffle is paid once.
- Adding workers to a job with too few partitions only adds idle cores.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Move to scikit-learn:** the number of files only limits the initial partition count and is cheap to change; a single driver gives up the distribution that the data size may need.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Spark ML tasks follow the partitions of the input. Repartitioning to a multiple of the cores spreads the passes over the whole cluster, and caching pays the shuffle once for all passes.
- ✗ **C. Driver memory:** the tasks run on executors and the idle cores are caused by too few partitions, not by driver memory.
- ✗ **D. More trees:** trees are built level by level over the partitions, not one task per tree, so the number of trees does not create tasks.

## Key idea
Spark ML uses as many cores as the DataFrame has partitions; repartition to a multiple of the cores and cache before fit.
Q011873:
## Use the learning curve
A learning curve plots validation error against training-set size. When the curve is flat, extra rows add cost without adding accuracy. Training on a representative sample on one node can then give the same quality at a fraction of the cost, and lets the team use an algorithm that is only available as a single-node library.
## Conditions for this trade-off
- The sample must be representative (stratified on the label or key segments if they are rare).
- The learning curve must be re-checked when the data or the problem changes, because the plateau can move.
- If rare segments need the full history, or the curve is still falling, Spark ML (or another distributed option) on the full table is justified.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** A sample past the plateau keeps accuracy, cuts compute from hours of cluster time to a single node, and lets the team keep XGBoost. Re-running the learning curve guards against distribution change.
- ✗ **B. 24 monthly models averaged:** this changes the problem (each model sees one month and misses seasonal or cross-month patterns) and the averaged ensemble is not a drop-in for the original model.
- ✗ **C. Add workers:** scaling out reduces wall-clock time but not cost per unit of accuracy, and it does not address that the extra data is not improving the model.
- ✗ **D. Train on all 1 TB:** the curve shows more rows do not lower validation error here, so the cost buys nothing and the team gives up its tuned model.

## Key idea
A flat learning curve means a representative sample on one node can match full-data distributed training at far lower cost.
Q011874:
## Where single-node libraries run
Libraries such as scikit-learn, XGBoost (single-node) and PyTorch on one device execute in the Python process where the code is called, which is the driver of a Databricks cluster. Spark does not distribute them automatically. A cluster with workers helps only if the code uses Spark APIs (Spark ML, Spark SQL, pandas function APIs) or a distributed framework (Ray, TorchDistributor, `joblibspark` for parallel trials).
## Options for using more machines
- Use one bigger single node when the data fits, since the fit then uses all of its cores.
- Switch to Spark ML (or a distributed variant of the algorithm) when the data no longer fits.
- Parallelize independent trials or per-group models, not one model fit, with pandas function APIs, Ray or Optuna on Spark.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Repartitioning:** partition count affects Spark jobs, but the scikit-learn fit does not run on Spark partitions at all, so repartitioning does not move the work.
- ✗ **B. n_jobs per executor:** `n_jobs` sets processes or threads inside the one Python process, not executors, and restarting executors changes nothing.
- ✗ **C. Config flag:** there is no such Spark setting; workers are already part of the cluster, they just are not used by non-Spark code.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** The fit is plain scikit-learn in the driver process, so extra workers sit idle. Choose a bigger single node, a distributed algorithm, or parallelize many independent fits.

## Key idea
Single-node libraries run on the driver only; extra workers help only with Spark or distributed frameworks.
Q011875:
## Distribution has overhead
A distributed algorithm splits rows over workers, computes partial results, and combines them over the network at every iteration or tree level. Scheduling tasks and moving partial results costs time that does not shrink with more workers. If one node holds the data and has enough cores, the single-node library avoids these costs.
## When the picture changes
- When data no longer fits in the memory of one node, single node is not an option and Spark ML scales better.
- When the number of rows or features grows large, the compute per iteration grows and the fixed overhead becomes small in comparison.
- A cluster-size increase helps only when per-task work, not overhead, is the bottleneck.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** With 5 GB the compute is small and the overhead of the distributed algorithm dominates, so the single node wins. Spark ML pays off when the data outgrows one machine.
- ✗ **B. More workers:** adding workers increases coordination, and for small data it can make the run slower rather than faster.
- ✗ **C. Driver-only trees:** Spark ML tree algorithms distribute the work to executors, which is why they scale to large data.
- ✗ **D. Always slower:** it is not true at every size. Past the memory limit of a single node, scikit-learn cannot run at all and Spark ML wins.

## Key idea
For data that fits on one node, distribution overhead makes a single node faster; Spark ML pays off beyond the memory of one machine.
Q011876:
## Missing values are learned state
`Imputer` is an `Estimator`. `fit` computes a surrogate value per column (mean by default, or median or mode) and returns an `ImputerModel` that stores them. All `null` and `NaN` values in the input columns are treated as missing and replaced. The input columns must be numeric.
## Why it belongs in the pipeline
- The fill values come from the training data and travel inside the saved `PipelineModel`, so scoring uses the same numbers without any copy.
- Median is robust to outliers, which matters for skewed columns such as income.
- Dropping rows (skip) changes the population: new customers with few records are lost, and a scoring job would silently return fewer predictions than it received.
- Imputers do not handle categorical features well: encode those with `StringIndexer` first.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. fillna(0) in notebooks:** a constant of 0 is a modelling choice that distorts income, and the call has to be repeated by hand in every scoring job, where the copies drift.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** The `Imputer` stage learns the medians at `fit` and keeps them in the `PipelineModel`, so every training and scoring batch gets the same fill values and no row is removed.
- ✗ **C. Hand-written SQL:** the training means are copied into every consumer, which is the training-serving mismatch that a stored `ImputerModel` avoids, and a mean is not robust to outliers.
- ✗ **D. Skipping rows:** invalid rows are removed, so the model never sees the new customers and scoring returns fewer rows than requested, which breaks joins on the output.

## Key idea
Use an Imputer stage so that the fill values are learned once and stored in the PipelineModel.
Q011877:
## Keep feature logic inside the pipeline
Anything computed outside the pipeline must be repeated by hand at scoring, and the two copies drift. Spark ML offers stateless `Transformer` stages for row-level logic. `SQLTransformer` runs a SQL statement in which `__THIS__` stands for the input DataFrame, so a derived column becomes a stage of the `Pipeline`. It is saved and loaded with the `PipelineModel`.
## Rules of thumb
- Row-level derived columns (ratios, flags, date parts): `SQLTransformer`.
- Anything that has to learn from the data (scaling, indexing, imputing): an Estimator stage whose fitted state is stored in the model.
- With ANSI mode on (the default in Spark 4), `clicks / impressions` raises an error when `impressions` is 0: write `try_divide(clicks, impressions)` in the stage to get NULL instead.
- Logic that cannot be expressed in a stage belongs in a documented, versioned feature pipeline, not in an ad hoc notebook cell.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Nightly job on the raw table:** this adds a second pipeline that must stay in step with the model, and the column stays absent for any source that is not that table.
- ✗ **B. Documenting the formula:** it relies on every consumer to reimplement it exactly, which is the training-serving mismatch the artifact is meant to avoid.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** The `SQLTransformer` stage makes `ctr` part of the saved `PipelineModel`, so training and scoring run the same formula from the same artifact.
- ✗ **D. Scoring-side UDF:** it duplicates the logic in a second place and can differ in null and division-by-zero handling from the notebook version.

## Key idea
Put row-level feature logic in the pipeline (SQLTransformer) so the saved PipelineModel reproduces it.
Q011878:
## Centering makes sparse data dense
`StandardScaler` has `withMean` set to false by default; centering subtracts the mean from every entry, so a sparse vector becomes dense. The Spark documentation warns that this builds a dense output. With 8 million dimensions per row, the dense output cannot be held in memory.
## Scalers that keep sparsity
- `MaxAbsScaler` rescales each feature to [-1, 1] by dividing through its maximum absolute value. It does not shift or center the data, and so it does not destroy any sparsity.
- `StandardScaler` with the default `withMean=False` scales to unit standard deviation only and also keeps sparse vectors sparse.
- `MinMaxScaler` subtracts the minimum, and `RobustScaler(withCentering=True)` subtracts the median, so both can make sparse vectors dense.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More memory for centering:** dense vectors of 8 million values per row are far beyond any realistic executor size, and the shift is not required to make the features comparable in scale.
- ✗ **B. MinMaxScaler:** it subtracts each feature's minimum before scaling, and any non-zero minimum turns zeros into non-zero values, which makes the vectors dense.
- ✗ **C. RobustScaler with centering:** removing the median is also a shift, and the documentation warns that centering builds a dense output.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** `MaxAbsScaler` only divides, so zero entries stay zero and the vectors stay sparse. It is an `Estimator`, so the maxima learned at `fit` are stored in the pipeline.

## Key idea
For high-dimensional sparse features, scale with MaxAbsScaler or StandardScaler without centering.
Q011879:
## Vector size in metadata
`VectorAssembler` needs the size of every input vector column to build output metadata. For a batch DataFrame, Spark can inspect the contents. In a streaming DataFrame, the contents are not available until the stream starts, so the size must come from column metadata.
## VectorSizeHint
`VectorSizeHint` is a transformer with `inputCol` and `size`. It adds the vector size to the column metadata so `VectorAssembler` and other stages can use that column. Its optional `handleInvalid` parameter controls vectors with nulls or the wrong size: `error` (default), `skip` (filter those rows) or `optimistic` (do not check, and so the metadata can disagree with the content).
- Put it directly before the stage that needs the size.
- Use `error` or `skip` rather than `optimistic` unless the producer is fully trusted.
- Fitting estimators still needs batch data: apply the fitted model to the stream with `transform`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** `VectorSizeHint` writes the known size of `emb` into the column metadata, so `VectorAssembler` can run on a streaming DataFrame without looking at the data.
- ✗ **B. VectorSlicer:** it selects entries by index and still depends on knowing the input vector, it does not declare the size of the column in the metadata.
- ✗ **C. Normalizer:** it rescales each vector to unit norm and leaves the column metadata without a declared vector length.
- ✗ **D. cache on a stream:** streaming DataFrames cannot be cached for batch inspection, and the contents appear only after the query starts.

## Key idea
Put VectorSizeHint before VectorAssembler when vector columns come from a streaming DataFrame.
Q011880:
## A Pipeline is an Estimator
A `Pipeline` has `fit` and returns a `PipelineModel`, so it is an `Estimator` and can be a stage in another `Pipeline`. The outer `fit` fits the nested pipeline (producing a nested `PipelineModel`) and passes its output to the later stages.
## Why this helps
- The shared featurization is defined in one place and versioned once.
- Each model pipeline is `Pipeline(stages=[featurization, classifier])`, so the saved outer `PipelineModel` is a single artifact that scores raw columns.
- Tuning with `CrossValidator` still re-fits the nested stages per fold, as needed to avoid leakage.
## When to separate
If many models must use the same fitted encodings (for instance, identical index values), fit the featurization once, save the `PipelineModel`, and reuse it as a transformer stage; accept that tuning then does not refit it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Collect and rebuild:** `collect()` moves the data to the driver, and rebuilding pipelines from rows throws away the fitted stage state and does not scale.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Using the featurization `Pipeline` as the first stage of each model pipeline keeps one definition and gives a self-contained artifact per model.
- ✗ **C. Fitted PipelineModel in the stage list:** a fitted `PipelineModel` is a `Transformer` and can be placed as a stage, but then it is fixed to the training data of the first fit, and the option as written replaces rather than reuses the definition.
- ✗ **D. Three stage copies:** sharing a stage definition is exactly what nesting a pipeline provides; copying objects gives three diverging definitions, and the claim about single-use is not a rule.

## Key idea
A Pipeline is an Estimator, so a shared featurization Pipeline can be the first stage of many model pipelines.
Q011881:
## Indices are learned state
`StringIndexer` is an `Estimator`: `fit` computes a mapping from category to index (by default ordered by frequency, most frequent first). When the data changes, frequencies and categories change, so the next `fit` can assign different numbers to the same category. A model trained on the old numbers then receives indices with a different meaning.
## Design consequences
- Treat indexed values as private to the fitted model, not as shared data. Store raw values and let each model's `PipelineModel` map them at scoring time.
- Alphabetical ordering makes the order deterministic for a fixed set of categories, but a new category still shifts alphabetical positions of the ones after it.
- If an indexed column must be shared, fit the indexer once, version the fitted model, and reuse it without refitting.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. maxCategories:** that is a `VectorIndexer` parameter for deciding which vector features are categorical, not a stability setting for `StringIndexer`.
- ✗ **B. Fit on a 10% sample:** the mapping depends on the content of the data used, not on the sample size, and a sample would miss rare categories too.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** The index mapping is part of each model's learned state. Keeping the raw category in the table, and mapping through the pipeline that the model was trained with, removes the dependence on refit order.
- ✗ **D. Alphabetical ordering:** it removes the frequency-based reordering, but any new category inserts a new index and shifts later ones, so old consumers can still break.

## Key idea
Index mappings are learned model state; share raw values and apply each model's own fitted pipeline.
Q011882:
## Labels must be numeric
Spark ML classifiers require a numeric label column of indices 0 to numClasses-1. A `StringIndexer` is an `Estimator`: `fit` learns the mapping from strings to indices (ordered by frequency by default) and returns a `StringIndexerModel`.
## Getting strings back
`IndexToString` is a `Transformer` that converts indices to the original labels, using either the metadata attached to the column by the indexer or an explicit `labels` list. Place it after the classifier, with `inputCol="prediction"`, and it appends the readable label. Because the mapping is stored in the fitted pipeline, the strings in the report always match the indices the model used.
- Use `StringIndexer` for labels and also for categorical features (before `OneHotEncoder` when needed).
- Never recreate the mapping by hand: any difference from the model's mapping silently mislabels predictions.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Bucketizer:** it bins numeric values with fixed splits; it cannot read strings, and a hand dictionary again leaves the mapping outside the pipeline.
- ✗ **B. Cast to int:** casting non-numeric strings gives null, so the label would be lost.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** The indexer learns the label mapping during `fit`, and `IndexToString` reverses it from the stored labels, so the whole path is inside the pipeline.
- ✗ **D. OneHotEncoder on the label:** Spark ML classifiers expect a single numeric index column as label, not a vector of dummy columns.

## Key idea
Use StringIndexer for string labels and IndexToString to turn predictions back into the original text.
Q011883:
## Estimator that learns, Transformer that applies
`Bucketizer` is a `Transformer`: you give it explicit `splits` and it maps values to bucket indices. `QuantileDiscretizer` is an `Estimator`: `fit` computes approximate quantiles of the input column and returns a `Bucketizer` model with those splits. The number of buckets can be smaller than requested if the input has too few distinct values.
## Why it matters for scoring
The splits are learned once from the training data and stored in the fitted `PipelineModel`. New batches are binned with the same boundaries, so a customer of a given age always lands in the same bin, and the model's learned coefficients stay valid.
- Use `Bucketizer` when the business defines the boundaries.
- Use `QuantileDiscretizer` when equal-frequency bins should be learned from training data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Repeated Binarizer:** `Binarizer` thresholds a value to 0/1 and thresholds are fixed numbers you must choose, so it does not learn quantiles and gives overlapping indicators rather than one bin.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** `QuantileDiscretizer` learns equal-frequency boundaries from the training data and freezes them in a `Bucketizer`, which the pipeline applies unchanged to later batches.
- ✗ **C. StandardScaler:** it centers and scales values; it does not bin, and z-scores are not equal-frequency groups.
- ✗ **D. Splits per scoring batch:** boundaries recomputed on each batch change the meaning of every bin between batches and break the model's learned weights.

## Key idea
QuantileDiscretizer (an Estimator) learns equal-frequency splits and keeps them as a Bucketizer; Bucketizer alone applies fixed splits.
Q011884:
## Two ways to build term-frequency vectors
- `HashingTF` is a `Transformer` that hashes each term into one of `numFeatures` buckets (default 2^18). It needs no global dictionary, which is cheap for huge corpora, but different words can share a bucket (collisions) and the word-to-position mapping is not stored.
- `CountVectorizer` is an `Estimator`: `fit` builds a vocabulary (limited by `vocabSize` and by document-frequency thresholds such as `minDF`) and the resulting model keeps `vocabulary`, so position i can be mapped back to a word.
## Trade-off
Hashing scales without a vocabulary pass and has fixed memory, but weights cannot be reliably named. If model explanations by word are required, use `CountVectorizer` and cap the vocabulary so that the vector size stays manageable.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Only `CountVectorizer` keeps the term list, so coefficients of the logistic regression can be matched to words; capping `vocabSize` and `minDF` handles the huge number of terms.
- ✗ **B. HashingTF with 2^10 buckets:** hashing never stores the words, and so few buckets cause heavy collisions that merge unrelated terms.
- ✗ **C. HashingTF with a huge size:** more buckets reduce collisions but cannot invert a hash; several words can still map to one index and the word is not recoverable.
- ✗ **D. IDF keeps names:** `IDF` learns inverse document frequencies per vector position; it holds no vocabulary, so it cannot name positions.

## Key idea
Use CountVectorizer when you must map weights back to words; HashingTF is stateless and cheap but not reversible.
Q011885:
## Cold start in ALS
`ALS` learns a latent factor vector for each user and item seen in training. A user or item that appears only in the validation data has no factors, so `transform` returns `NaN` for those rows. By default (`coldStartStrategy="nan"`) the NaN stays in the predictions, so an evaluator averaging them returns `NaN` and model selection becomes impossible.
## The documented remedy
Setting `coldStartStrategy="drop"` drops prediction rows with NaN, so the metric is computed on the remaining rows only.
- Report the share of dropped rows, because dropping makes the metric optimistic when many users are new.
- For production cold start, combine ALS with a popularity or content-based fallback; ALS alone cannot rank unseen users.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. rank 200:** a larger rank adds capacity for known users and items, but unseen ones still have no factor vector.
- ✗ **B. nonnegative:** it constrains factors to be non-negative; it does not create factors for unknown users.
- ✗ **C. mae:** any metric computed over NaN predictions is NaN; the metric name is not the cause.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** With `coldStartStrategy="drop"` the NaN predictions for unseen users and items are removed, so RMSE is computed on the rest and the cross-validation can pick a model.

## Key idea
Use coldStartStrategy="drop" for ALS evaluation, and watch how many rows are dropped.
Q011886:
## KMeans uses distances
KMeans assigns each point to the nearest centroid by Euclidean distance. A feature with a numeric range of hundreds of thousands dominates the distance, so the clusters reflect it and ignore a feature with range 0 to 30.
## Scale first
`StandardScaler` is an `Estimator` that learns each feature's mean and standard deviation (`withStd` is true by default, `withMean` is false by default, because centering a sparse vector makes it dense) and produces a `StandardScalerModel`. Put it between `VectorAssembler` and `KMeans` in the pipeline, and its learned statistics are reused when new customers are assigned to clusters.
- Evaluate with `ClusteringEvaluator` (silhouette score) and compare values of k.
- Tree-based models are insensitive to scale; distance-based models (KMeans, KNN, regularized linear models) are not.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. LogisticRegression:** it is a supervised classifier, and there are no labels in this clustering task.
- ✗ **B. More iterations:** KMeans converges to a local optimum under the same distance; more iterations do not change the weighting of features.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Standardizing puts both features on a comparable scale, so the distance reflects both and the visit pattern can shape the clusters.
- ✗ **D. Larger k:** more clusters subdivide the income axis further; the unscaled distance still ignores the small-range feature.

## Key idea
Scale features before distance-based algorithms such as KMeans.
Q011887:
## Selectors in Spark ML
- `UnivariateFeatureSelector` picks a score function from the types you set: categorical features with a categorical label use chi-squared; continuous features with a categorical label use the ANOVA F-test; continuous features with a continuous label use the F-value (regression). Selection modes include `numTopFeatures`, `percentile` and `fpr`. It is an `Estimator`: it learns which feature indices to keep.
- `ChiSqSelector` is the older chi-squared selector for categorical features.
- `VarianceThresholdSelector` removes low-variance features without using the label.
- `PCA` creates new combined components, not a subset of the original features.
## Pipeline placement
Put the selector after `VectorAssembler` and fit it inside the cross-validated pipeline, because it uses the label and can leak validation information if fitted on the whole set.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. PCA:** PCA outputs 200 new components that mix features, not the 200 most associated original features, and it does not use the label.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Continuous features with a categorical label call for the ANOVA F-test, which `UnivariateFeatureSelector` applies with `numTopFeatures=200`.
- ✗ **C. ChiSqSelector for continuous features:** chi-squared expects categorical features, and its statistic is not a correlation.
- ✗ **D. VarianceThresholdSelector:** it ignores the label and keeps features by variance, so it does not measure association with the 4 classes.

## Key idea
For continuous features with a categorical label, use UnivariateFeatureSelector (ANOVA) inside the cross-validated pipeline.
Q011888:
## Random folds leak groups
`CrossValidator` splits rows at random. If one customer's transactions are spread over the folds, the model sees that customer in training and is then validated on the same customer, memorizing customer-specific patterns. Scores are optimistic for new customers, which is the production situation.
## foldCol
`CrossValidator` accepts `foldCol`, a column with user-specified fold numbers. Spark then skips random k-fold and uses your assignment. The column must be an integer in the range 0 to numFolds-1; out-of-range values raise an error. Assigning folds by a hash of the group key keeps all rows of a customer in the same fold.
- Make the fold assignment deterministic and independent of the label.
- Check fold sizes: very uneven groups give uneven folds.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** `foldCol` with a customer-based fold number makes every customer appear in only one validation fold, so the score measures performance on unseen customers.
- ✗ **B. Fixed seed:** a seed makes the random folds repeatable but they stay random with respect to customers.
- ✗ **C. TrainValidationSplit:** it also splits rows at random into train and validation, so customers are still shared; it has no foldCol.
- ✗ **D. More folds:** the leakage comes from customers spread over folds, and smaller folds do not keep a customer together.

## Key idea
For grouped data, assign folds by group with foldCol so that no group is split across training and validation.
Q011889:
## What parallelism does
By default `CrossValidator` and `TrainValidationSplit` evaluate parameter settings in serial. `setParallelism(n)` with n of 2 or more fits n models concurrently. The Spark documentation advises choosing a value that maximizes parallelism without exceeding cluster resources, notes that larger values may not improve performance, and says a value up to 10 is generally sufficient.
## Interaction with a big fit
If each fit already uses the whole cluster, running more fits at once only shares the same cores and memory, so there is no gain and memory pressure increases (each concurrent fit caches its data and tree statistics).
- Raise parallelism when each fit is small compared with the cluster (small data, few partitions).
- Keep it at 1 to 2 when each fit is large.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Not allowed for trees:** parallelism is a general setting and works for any estimator; the problem is resource contention.
- ✗ **B. Only validation:** the parameter evaluates complete fit-and-evaluate runs for different parameter settings, which includes training.
- ✗ **C. Minimum of 64:** there is no minimum tied to workers times cores; the value is the number of concurrent model fits, and the documentation says up to 10 is generally enough.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Concurrent fits compete for the same executors and memory, so a large single fit leaves no spare capacity; a small value matches what the cluster can hold.

## Key idea
Parallelism is the number of concurrent fits; it helps only when each fit leaves spare cluster capacity.
Q011890:
## Tuning without labels
`CrossValidator` and `TrainValidationSplit` need an `Evaluator` whose metric tells which `ParamMap` is better. Classification and regression evaluators compare predictions with a label column, which an unsupervised task does not have. `ClusteringEvaluator` computes the silhouette score (by default with squared Euclidean distance) from the feature vectors and the cluster assignments only.
## Cautions
- The silhouette score is a larger-is-better measure, so no change of direction is needed.
- It is distance based: scale the features before `KMeans` and before evaluating, otherwise one feature decides the score.
- The score usually changes little between neighbouring values of `k`: also consider the business use and the cost of the cluster count.
- At 80 million rows, `TrainValidationSplit` fits each `k` once, while `CrossValidator` would multiply the cost by the number of folds.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. f1 on random labels:** the metric would compare cluster numbers with noise, and cluster indices have no fixed meaning that could match any label.
- ✗ **B. RMSE on the cluster index:** the index is an arbitrary identifier, so a difference between two identifiers carries no information about fit.
- ✗ **C. BinaryClassificationEvaluator:** it needs a true label and a raw prediction column, and clusters are not positive and negative classes.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** `ClusteringEvaluator` measures cluster separation without labels, so the grid over `k` can be scored and the best model chosen by the highest silhouette.

## Key idea
Tune unsupervised models with an evaluator that needs no label, such as ClusteringEvaluator.
Q011891:
## MLlib tuning takes a list of ParamMaps
`CrossValidator` and `TrainValidationSplit` need an `Estimator`, a list of `ParamMap`s (`estimatorParamMaps`) and an `Evaluator`. `ParamGridBuilder` builds the full Cartesian product of the lists given with `addGrid`. It has no random mode.
## Random search with MLlib
Since `estimatorParamMaps` is just a list, you can build it yourself: draw 40 combinations from your distributions and create one `ParamMap` per draw (a dict from estimator params to values). The evaluator and cross-validation logic stay the same.
- Random search often finds a good region with far fewer fits than a full grid when only a few hyperparameters matter.
- For adaptive search (Bayesian, early stopping), use a tuning library such as Optuna instead.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. numFolds=40:** `numFolds` sets how the data is split for validation, not how many parameter combinations are tried.
- ✗ **B. Distributions in addGrid:** `addGrid` takes a list of values, not a distribution object, and `CrossValidator` does no sampling.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Because `estimatorParamMaps` accepts any list of `ParamMap`s, 40 sampled combinations can be passed in directly and evaluated by the normal cross-validation.
- ✗ **D. setRandom:** the builder has no such method; it enumerates every combination of the values added.

## Key idea
MLlib has only grid generation; for random search, pass your own sampled list of ParamMaps.
Q011892:
## Time order must be respected
In forecasting, the model is used on dates after its training data. A random split lets the model train on rows from after a validation row, and neighboring days are strongly correlated, so validation rows have near duplicates in training. The score is then far better than the error on truly future data.
## What to do in Spark ML
Spark ML has no time-series cross-validation. Split by a timestamp: train on the earlier period and validate on the later one (and repeat over several cut-off dates if needed), then compare parameter maps on the later period. A hold-out final test on the newest period gives the estimate for deployment.
- Lag and rolling features must be computed using only earlier rows.
- `foldCol` can group rows into time blocks, but it still trains on blocks that are later than the validation block, so it is not a replacement.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Bigger grid:** more combinations do not remove leakage from the split and can overfit it further.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Splitting by time prevents the training data from containing the future of the validation rows, so the metric reflects forward-looking performance.
- ✗ **C. Shuffling more:** the random mixing is the problem; shuffling or using more folds adds more future rows to training.
- ✗ **D. Evaluator invalid:** `RegressionEvaluator` works on any numeric predictions; the issue is how the data was split.

## Key idea
For time-dependent data, validate on a later period than training; random folds leak the future.
Q011893:
## What avgMetrics contains
`CrossValidatorModel.avgMetrics` has one value per `ParamMap`: the metric averaged over the folds for that setting. The best value is the maximum of many noisy estimates, and the parameters were picked because of it, so it is optimistically biased as an estimate of the final quality.
## Honest estimate
- Split off a test set first (for instance with `randomSplit` and a seed, or by time).
- Run cross-validation on the training part only.
- Evaluate `cvModel.bestModel`, the `Pipeline` model refit on the whole training part with the best parameters, once on the test set.
The same applies to `TrainValidationSplit`. Training-set scores say nothing about generalization.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** A test set untouched by tuning gives an unbiased estimate; `bestModel` is evaluated on it once and that figure goes in the model card.
- ✗ **B. Maximum is unbiased:** selecting the maximum over many candidates on the same folds is a form of selection bias, so it overstates quality.
- ✗ **C. Training score:** fitted models score best on data they have seen, so this gives the most optimistic number.
- ✗ **D. Average of avgMetrics:** the mean over all parameter maps mixes good and poor settings and describes no deployable model.

## Key idea
Report the score of the best model on a test set not used for tuning, not the best cross-validation metric.
